args.research_question: Within the STEAD three-component traces labeled 'noise' (no cataloged source), what fraction exhibit statistically anomalous, cross-component-coherent transient energy bursts -- with polarization and STA/LTA signatures resembling a genuine body-wave arrival rather than incoherent stationary background -- and does this prevalence differ systematically by channel/instrument type (BH/EH/HH/HN/SH) or network?
args.hypothesis: A non-trivial minority of nominally noise-labeled STEAD traces (predicted roughly 5-15%) contain coherent, polarized transient bursts statistically indistinguishable, in STA/LTA amplitude ratio and rectilinearity/planarity at onset, from genuine earthquake arrivals calibrated on the labeled earthquake subset; this 'contamination' rate is not uniform across instrument/channel types, being higher for accelerometer/short-period channels (HN, EH, SH) that are more sensitive to anthropogenic/cultural transients than for broadband channels (BH, HH).
args.experiment: (1) For every trace (both labels, ~1500), compute per-channel STA/LTA characteristic functions (e.g. 0.5 s / 10 s windows) and record the maximum ratio and its onset sample per component. (2) At each candidate onset, compute the 3-component covariance matrix in a short sliding window and extract its eigenvalue-based rectilinearity and planarity (polarization attributes), plus cross-channel onset-time coincidence (all three components peaking within +-0.2 s). (3) Combine these into a single anomaly/coherence score per trace. (4) Build a label-agnostic null distribution for this score by generating synthetic 3-component colored-noise surrogates whose power spectral density is matched (via phase randomization / IAAFT) to each real noise-labeled trace's own PSD, run the identical pipeline on the surrogates, and set a detection threshold at a fixed false-alarm rate (e.g. 1%) purely from this synthetic null -- no label is used in choosing the threshold. (5) Apply that label-agnostic threshold to the real noise-labeled traces to estimate the 'anomalous transient' prevalence and its false-positive rate (known by construction from the null). (6) Separately, and only for post-hoc calibration/attribution (not decision-making), compare the score distributions of the labeled earthquake vs. labeled noise subsets to show the anomalous-noise scores overlap the earthquake distribution's lower tail. (7) Cross-tabulate the label-agnostic-flagged noise traces by channel code and network using chi-square/Fisher tests to test for non-uniform prevalence.
args.what_would_falsify: If the label-agnostic anomaly score for noise-labeled traces stays within the synthetic-null false-alarm rate (e.g. ~1% flagged, matching the calibration target) with no excess above it, and/or the earthquake and noise score distributions are cleanly separated with no overlap, this falsifies the contamination hypothesis and instead supports STEAD's noise class being clean, incoherent background across channel types.
args.minimal_publishable_claim: Even if the predicted instrument-type dependence is not confirmed, a rigorously calibrated (label-agnostic, null-model-referenced) measurement of the actual prevalence of coherent transient contamination in STEAD's noise class is itself a useful, previously unreported quality-control statistic for a widely used benchmark.
args.novelty_evidence: Searches for 'STEAD noise mislabeled/contamination', 'shortcut learning/artifact bias in seismic datasets', and 'STA/LTA or polarization detection of hidden events in noise windows' returned only tangential results: reviews of ML in seismology (Mousavi & Beroza 2022; Kubo et al. 2024), phase-picker methods papers (OBSTransformer, PickBlue), classic polarization-filter methodology (Schimmel & Gallart 2003), and unrelated cross-domain 'label noise' ML papers (face datasets, histopathology). No study surfaced that specifically audits STEAD's noise partition for embedded coherent transients broken down by instrument/channel type, supporting that this angle is under-explored, though the underlying single-station detection tools are classic.
args.what_data_cannot_establish: This analysis can only establish, from the waveform samples themselves, whether coherent/polarized transient energy statistically exceeding a noise-matched null is present in traces labeled 'noise' and how its prevalence associates with channel/network metadata; it cannot determine the physical origin of any flagged transient (uncatalogued small earthquake vs. quarry blast vs. cultural/anthropogenic noise vs. instrument glitch) without independent catalog cross-referencing or origin-time/location information that is not available in this dataset, nor can it make any claim about detector performance on data beyond STEAD.
args.effective_sample_estimate: Approximately 750 noise-labeled and 750 earthquake-labeled traces (balanced mix per the dataset description). At a predicted 5-15% contamination rate, this yields roughly 37-112 flagged 'anomalous noise' traces -- enough for a chi-square/Fisher-exact breakdown by channel code (5 categories) and by network, provided channel/network counts are checked for adequate cell sizes (pooling rare categories if needed); this is far more decisive than relying on a handful of hand-picked examples, since the score is continuous and computed on the full subset rather than only on a few visually flagged cases.
args.leakage_check: The anomaly-detection threshold is calibrated exclusively from synthetic PSD-matched noise surrogates (a label-agnostic null model with a known, fixed false-alarm rate), never from the earthquake-labeled traces or from the noise label itself; the label field is used only afterward, for reporting prevalence and cross-tabulating by channel/network, and for a secondary oracle-only comparison (earthquake vs noise score distributions) that is explicitly flagged as post-hoc calibration/attribution, not as part of the detection decision.

args.hypothesis: A non-trivial minority of nominally noise-labeled STEAD traces (predicted roughly 5-15%) contain coherent, polarized transient bursts statistically indistinguishable, in STA/LTA amplitude ratio and rectilinearity/planarity at onset, from genuine earthquake arrivals calibrated on the labeled earthquake subset; this 'contamination' rate is not uniform across instrument/channel types, being higher for accelerometer/short-period channels (HN, EH, SH) that are more sensitive to anthropogenic/cultural transients than for broadband channels (BH, HH).
args.experiment: (1) For every trace (both labels, ~1500), compute per-channel STA/LTA characteristic functions (e.g. 0.5 s / 10 s windows) and record the maximum ratio and its onset sample per component. (2) At each candidate onset, compute the 3-component covariance matrix in a short sliding window and extract its eigenvalue-based rectilinearity and planarity (polarization attributes), plus cross-channel onset-time coincidence (all three components peaking within +-0.2 s). (3) Combine these into a single anomaly/coherence score per trace. (4) Build a label-agnostic null distribution for this score by generating synthetic 3-component colored-noise surrogates whose power spectral density is matched (via phase randomization / IAAFT) to each real noise-labeled trace's own PSD, run the identical pipeline on the surrogates, and set a detection threshold at a fixed false-alarm rate (e.g. 1%) purely from this synthetic null -- no label is used in choosing the threshold. (5) Apply that label-agnostic threshold to the real noise-labeled traces to estimate the 'anomalous transient' prevalence and its false-positive rate (known by construction from the null). (6) Separately, and only for post-hoc calibration/attribution (not decision-making), compare the score distributions of the labeled earthquake vs. labeled noise subsets to show the anomalous-noise scores overlap the earthquake distribution's lower tail. (7) Cross-tabulate the label-agnostic-flagged noise traces by channel code and network using chi-square/Fisher tests to test for non-uniform prevalence.
args.what_would_falsify: If the label-agnostic anomaly score for noise-labeled traces stays within the synthetic-null false-alarm rate (e.g. ~1% flagged, matching the calibration target) with no excess above it, and/or the earthquake and noise score distributions are cleanly separated with no overlap, this falsifies the contamination hypothesis and instead supports STEAD's noise class being clean, incoherent background across channel types.
args.minimal_publishable_claim: Even if the predicted instrument-type dependence is not confirmed, a rigorously calibrated (label-agnostic, null-model-referenced) measurement of the actual prevalence of coherent transient contamination in STEAD's noise class is itself a useful, previously unreported quality-control statistic for a widely used benchmark.
args.novelty_evidence: Searches for 'STEAD noise mislabeled/contamination', 'shortcut learning/artifact bias in seismic datasets', and 'STA/LTA or polarization detection of hidden events in noise windows' returned only tangential results: reviews of ML in seismology (Mousavi & Beroza 2022; Kubo et al. 2024), phase-picker methods papers (OBSTransformer, PickBlue), classic polarization-filter methodology (Schimmel & Gallart 2003), and unrelated cross-domain 'label noise' ML papers (face datasets, histopathology). No study surfaced that specifically audits STEAD's noise partition for embedded coherent transients broken down by instrument/channel type, supporting that this angle is under-explored, though the underlying single-station detection tools are classic.
args.what_data_cannot_establish: This analysis can only establish, from the waveform samples themselves, whether coherent/polarized transient energy statistically exceeding a noise-matched null is present in traces labeled 'noise' and how its prevalence associates with channel/network metadata; it cannot determine the physical origin of any flagged transient (uncatalogued small earthquake vs. quarry blast vs. cultural/anthropogenic noise vs. instrument glitch) without independent catalog cross-referencing or origin-time/location information that is not available in this dataset, nor can it make any claim about detector performance on data beyond STEAD.
args.effective_sample_estimate: Approximately 750 noise-labeled and 750 earthquake-labeled traces (balanced mix per the dataset description). At a predicted 5-15% contamination rate, this yields roughly 37-112 flagged 'anomalous noise' traces -- enough for a chi-square/Fisher-exact breakdown by channel code (5 categories) and by network, provided channel/network counts are checked for adequate cell sizes (pooling rare categories if needed); this is far more decisive than relying on a handful of hand-picked examples, since the score is continuous and computed on the full subset rather than only on a few visually flagged cases.
args.leakage_check: The anomaly-detection threshold is calibrated exclusively from synthetic PSD-matched noise surrogates (a label-agnostic null model with a known, fixed false-alarm rate), never from the earthquake-labeled traces or from the noise label itself; the label field is used only afterward, for reporting prevalence and cross-tabulating by channel/network, and for a secondary oracle-only comparison (earthquake vs noise score distributions) that is explicitly flagged as post-hoc calibration/attribution, not as part of the detection decision.
args.visual_audit: Confirmed given labels (from list_materials sample_records) were only available for idx 0 (earthquake), idx 1 (noise), idx 2 (earthquake). Viewed idx0: sharp, large 3-component onset with clean coda -- consistent with its earthquake label. Viewed idx2: sharp onset ~sample 1050-1100 on all channels -- consistent with its earthquake label. Viewed idx1 (given label 'noise'): the rendering showed a clear amplitude buildup and decay (a transient-looking envelope) between samples ~2500-4000, which visually disagrees with a 'pure stationary ambient noise' expectation for that label. I did not override the given label -- I kept it as 'noise' per the data -- but flagged this mismatch explicitly, and it directly motivated the selected research question (systematically auditing how often noise-labeled traces contain such coherent transient-like envelopes, using a label-agnostic synthetic-null threshold rather than trusting visual impression or the label itself). Additional indices (3,5,7,9,11) were inspected for exploratory pattern-scouting (to gauge general variability of transient-like envelopes across the set), but their tool outputs did not explicitly redisplay a confirmed given label to reconcile against, so I do not report these as confirmed label agreements/disagreements -- they informed pipeline design only (e.g., recognizing that onset sharpness, cross-channel coincidence, and envelope buildup/decay are the discriminating features to encode), not any labeled-group characterization.

args.method_summary: Dataset: 1500 STEAD 3-component (100 Hz, 60s, 6000-sample) traces, balanced 750 earthquake / 750 noise, spanning channel codes BH(311)/EH(272)/HH(704)/HN(205)/SH(8) and >50 networks. For every trace and each of the 3 components we compute an STA/LTA characteristic function (0.5s STA / 10s LTA, variance-floored to avoid division blow-ups on near-flat segments; channels with std<1e-6 flagged as dead and excluded from the 3-component vote). Per trace we take the per-channel STA/LTA peak (log1p-compressed amplitude term), the spread of the three per-channel onset times converted to a soft coincidence term exp(-spread/0.2s), and, in a +-1s window around the median onset, the 3-channel covariance-matrix eigenvalues giving rectilinearity R=1-lambda2/lambda1 and planarity P=1-2*lambda3/(lambda1+lambda2). The combined anomaly score = log_amp * R * P * soft_coincidence. A label-agnostic null is built per noise trace via three independent surrogate families (primary: IAAFT per-channel, matching each channel's own marginal distribution and power spectrum but destroying cross-channel phase coherence; secondary: simple phase-randomization; tertiary: variance-matched white Gaussian noise), run through the identical pipeline; the detection threshold is the 99th percentile of the surrogate score distribution (nominal FAR=1%), with no label information used in setting it. This threshold is applied to the real noise-labeled traces to estimate prevalence, with a binomial 95% CI and a station-cluster bootstrap (resampling by unique network+station group, since 178/417 stations contribute >1 trace) to check group non-independence. Ablations remove score components (coincidence, rectilinearity, planarity, or all polarization) one at a time; sensitivity analyses vary the FAR (0.1%-5%), the null-model type, and the STA/LTA window (0.2-1.0s / 5-20s). Breakdown analyses cross-tabulate flagged status by channel type and by network (chi-square tests, networks/channels with n>=15/20). A post-hoc-only comparison (not used for any threshold decision) compares flagged-noise, unflagged-noise, and labeled-earthquake score distributions to check for overlap with the earthquake tail.
args.stat_tests: 7 total formal hypothesis tests were run: chi2 channel breakdown, chi2 network breakdown, and 4 Mann-Whitney U tests (onset spread, rectilinearity R, planarity P, log-amplitude, flagged vs unflagged noise) plus 1 point-biserial correlation (flag status vs station-repeat-count, leakage check). 01_ideation.json.known_landscape: STEAD (Mousavi et al.) is a standard benchmark for ML phase pickers/detectors; extensive literature (Mousavi & Beroza 2022 review; OBSTransformer; PickBlue; Zhu et al. augmentation work) uses its earthquake/noise split as ground truth for training/testing detectors, generally treating the "noise" class as clean stationary background. Polarization/rectilinearity analysis (Schimmel & Gallart 2003) and STA/LTA detection are well-established single-station tools for identifying and characterizing transient body-wave arrivals, but I found no study that systematically audits STEAD's noise-labeled partition itself for embedded coherent transient energy, nor one that quantifies how such contamination is distributed across instrument/channel types. Searches on 'STEAD noise mislabeled', 'shortcut learning seismic dataset artifact', and 'STA/LTA hidden events in noise windows' returned no directly matching prior work (only tangential ML-bias literature from other domains and general polarization-filter papers), suggesting this specific audit is under-explored.

01_ideation.json.hypothesis: A non-trivial minority of nominally noise-labeled STEAD traces (predicted roughly 5-15%) contain coherent, polarized transient bursts statistically indistinguishable, in STA/LTA amplitude ratio and rectilinearity/planarity at onset, from genuine earthquake arrivals calibrated on the labeled earthquake subset; this 'contamination' rate is not uniform across instrument/channel types, being higher for accelerometer/short-period channels (HN, EH, SH) that are more sensitive to anthropogenic/cultural transients than for broadband channels (BH, HH).
01_ideation.json.experiment: (1) For every trace (both labels, ~1500), compute per-channel STA/LTA characteristic functions (e.g. 0.5 s / 10 s windows) and record the maximum ratio and its onset sample per component. (2) At each candidate onset, compute the 3-component covariance matrix in a short sliding window and extract its eigenvalue-based rectilinearity and planarity (polarization attributes), plus cross-channel onset-time coincidence (all three components peaking within +-0.2 s). (3) Combine these into a single anomaly/coherence score per trace. (4) Build a label-agnostic null distribution for this score by generating synthetic 3-component colored-noise surrogates whose power spectral density is matched (via phase randomization / IAAFT) to each real noise-labeled trace's own PSD, run the identical pipeline on the surrogates, and set a detection threshold at a fixed false-alarm rate (e.g. 1%) purely from this synthetic null -- no label is used in choosing the threshold. (5) Apply that label-agnostic threshold to the real noise-labeled traces to estimate the 'anomalous transient' prevalence and its false-positive rate (known by construction from the null). (6) Separately, and only for post-hoc calibration/attribution (not decision-making), compare the score distributions of the labeled earthquake vs. labeled noise subsets to show the anomalous-noise scores overlap the earthquake distribution's lower tail. (7) Cross-tabulate the label-agnostic-flagged noise traces by channel code and network using chi-square/Fisher tests to test for non-uniform prevalence.
01_ideation.json.what_would_falsify: If the label-agnostic anomaly score for noise-labeled traces stays within the synthetic-null false-alarm rate (e.g. ~1% flagged, matching the calibration target) with no excess above it, and/or the earthquake and noise score distributions are cleanly separated with no overlap, this falsifies the contamination hypothesis and instead supports STEAD's noise class being clean, incoherent background across channel types.
01_ideation.json.minimal_publishable_claim: Even if the predicted instrument-type dependence is not confirmed, a rigorously calibrated (label-agnostic, null-model-referenced) measurement of the actual prevalence of coherent transient contamination in STEAD's noise class is itself a useful, previously unreported quality-control statistic for a widely used benchmark.
01_ideation.json.novelty_evidence: Searches for 'STEAD noise mislabeled/contamination', 'shortcut learning/artifact bias in seismic datasets', and 'STA/LTA or polarization detection of hidden events in noise windows' returned only tangential results: reviews of ML in seismology (Mousavi & Beroza 2022; Kubo et al. 2024), phase-picker methods papers (OBSTransformer, PickBlue), classic polarization-filter methodology (Schimmel & Gallart 2003), and unrelated cross-domain 'label noise' ML papers (face datasets, histopathology). No study surfaced that specifically audits STEAD's noise partition for embedded coherent transients broken down by instrument/channel type, supporting that this angle is under-explored, though the underlying single-station detection tools are classic.
01_ideation.json.what_data_cannot_establish: This analysis can only establish, from the waveform samples themselves, whether coherent/polarized transient energy statistically exceeding a noise-matched null is present in traces labeled 'noise' and how its prevalence associates with channel/network metadata; it cannot determine the physical origin of any flagged transient (uncatalogued small earthquake vs. quarry blast vs. cultural/anthropogenic noise vs. instrument glitch) without independent catalog cross-referencing or origin-time/location information that is not available in this dataset, nor can it make any claim about detector performance on data beyond STEAD.
01_ideation.json.effective_sample_estimate: Approximately 750 noise-labeled and 750 earthquake-labeled traces (balanced mix per the dataset description). At a predicted 5-15% contamination rate, this yields roughly 37-112 flagged 'anomalous noise' traces -- enough for a chi-square/Fisher-exact breakdown by channel code (5 categories) and by network, provided channel/network counts are checked for adequate cell sizes (pooling rare categories if needed); this is far more decisive than relying on a handful of hand-picked examples, since the score is continuous and computed on the full subset rather than only on a few visually flagged cases.
01_ideation.json.leakage_check: The anomaly-detection threshold is calibrated exclusively from synthetic PSD-matched noise surrogates (a label-agnostic null model with a known, fixed false-alarm rate), never from the earthquake-labeled traces or from the noise label itself; the label field is used only afterward, for reporting prevalence and cross-tabulating by channel/network, and for a secondary oracle-only comparison (earthquake vs noise score distributions) that is explicitly flagged as post-hoc calibration/attribution, not as part of the detection decision.
01_ideation.json.visual_audit: Confirmed given labels (from list_materials sample_records) were only available for idx 0 (earthquake), idx 1 (noise), idx 2 (earthquake). Viewed idx0: sharp, large 3-component onset with clean coda -- consistent with its earthquake label. Viewed idx2: sharp onset ~sample 1050-1100 on all channels -- consistent with its earthquake label. Viewed idx1 (given label 'noise'): the rendering showed a clear amplitude buildup and decay (a transient-looking envelope) between samples ~2500-4000, which visually disagrees with a 'pure stationary ambient noise' expectation for that label. I did not override the given label -- I kept it as 'noise' per the data -- but flagged this mismatch explicitly, and it directly motivated the selected research question (systematically auditing how often noise-labeled traces contain such coherent transient-like envelopes, using a label-agnostic synthetic-null threshold rather than trusting visual impression or the label itself). Additional indices (3,5,7,9,11) were inspected for exploratory pattern-scouting (to gauge general variability of transient-like envelopes across the set), but their tool outputs did not explicitly redisplay a confirmed given label to reconcile against, so I do not report these as confirmed label agreements/disagreements -- they informed pipeline design only (e.g., recognizing that onset sharpness, cross-channel coincidence, and envelope buildup/decay are the discriminating features to encode), not any labeled-group characterization.

analyses.finding: Label-agnostic (IAAFT-null-calibrated, 1% FAR) detector flags 21.7% of noise-labeled STEAD traces as containing coherent, polarized, cross-component-coincident transient bursts indistinguishable from body-wave-like arrivals

analyses.name: baseline
analyses.finding: An amplitude-only STA/LTA detector (no polarization/coincidence gating) calibrated to the same 1% FAR flags only 2.0% of noise traces -- 10x lower than the full coherence-aware score, showing the polarization+coincidence machinery is essential, not just amplitude excursions

analyses.name: ablation
analyses.finding: Removing the coincidence term collapses prevalence to baseline levels (2.0%); removing polarization (R,P) or removing either R or P alone barely changes prevalence (~21-22%) -- coincidence (cross-channel onset timing) is the dominant driver of the score, not polarization shape

02_experiment.json.method_summary: Dataset: 1500 STEAD 3-component (100 Hz, 60s, 6000-sample) traces, balanced 750 earthquake / 750 noise, spanning channel codes BH(311)/EH(272)/HH(704)/HN(205)/SH(8) and >50 networks. For every trace and each of the 3 components we compute an STA/LTA characteristic function (0.5s STA / 10s LTA, variance-floored to avoid division blow-ups on near-flat segments; channels with std<1e-6 flagged as dead and excluded from the 3-component vote). Per trace we take the per-channel STA/LTA peak (log1p-compressed amplitude term), the spread of the three per-channel onset times converted to a soft coincidence term exp(-spread/0.2s), and, in a +-1s window around the median onset, the 3-channel covariance-matrix eigenvalues giving rectilinearity R=1-lambda2/lambda1 and planarity P=1-2*lambda3/(lambda1+lambda2). The combined anomaly score = log_amp * R * P * soft_coincidence. A label-agnostic null is built per noise trace via three independent surrogate families (primary: IAAFT per-channel, matching each channel's own marginal distribution and power spectrum but destroying cross-channel phase coherence; secondary: simple phase-randomization; tertiary: variance-matched white Gaussian noise), run through the identical pipeline; the detection threshold is the 99th percentile of the surrogate score distribution (nominal FAR=1%), with no label information used in setting it. This threshold is applied to the real noise-labeled traces to estimate prevalence, with a binomial 95% CI and a station-cluster bootstrap (resampling by unique network+station group, since 178/417 stations contribute >1 trace) to check group non-independence. Ablations remove score components (coincidence, rectilinearity, planarity, or all polarization) one at a time; sensitivity analyses vary the FAR (0.1%-5%), the null-model type, and the STA/LTA window (0.2-1.0s / 5-20s). Breakdown analyses cross-tabulate flagged status by channel type and by network (chi-square tests, networks/channels with n>=15/20). A post-hoc-only comparison (not used for any threshold decision) compares flagged-noise, unflagged-noise, and labeled-earthquake score distributions to check for overlap with the earthquake tail.
02_experiment.json.stat_tests: 7 total formal hypothesis tests were run: chi2 channel breakdown, chi2 network breakdown, and 4 Mann-Whitney U tests (onset spread, rectilinearity R, planarity P, log-amplitude, flagged vs unflagged noise) plus 1 point-biserial correlation (flag status vs station-repeat-count, leakage check). Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (alpha=0.05) and Bonferroni (alpha=0.0071) were applied to this set of 7 p-values; all 7 survive both corrections (largest raw p=0.00216 for the leakage-check correlation, still far below both thresholds; the mechanism p-values range from 4.9E-17 to 1.3E-84, all far below threshold).
02_experiment.json.independence_check: The anomaly score (log-amplitude x rectilinearity x planarity x cross-channel coincidence, computed directly from raw 3-component waveforms) and the detection threshold (99th percentile of the SAME score computed on synthetic surrogates of each trace, not on labels) are independent of the STEAD noise/earthquake label -- the label is used only afterward, for post-hoc calibration/attribution and for the channel/network breakdown, never for choosing the score formula or the threshold. This makes the prevalence estimate label-agnostic and non-circular. However, the null is generated per-trace from that same trace's own spectral content (IAAFT/phase-randomization), so the comparison is within-representation (same STA/LTA+polarization pipeline) rather than against a fully independent model; the claim is scoped accordingly to a label-agnostic, null-referenced, within-pipeline prevalence estimate, not an externally validated ground truth.
02_experiment.json.result_statement: The lead finding is that a rigorously calibrated, fully label-agnostic anomaly score (STA/LTA amplitude x rectilinearity x planarity x cross-channel onset coincidence, thresholded at a 1% false-alarm rate purely from IAAFT-matched synthetic nulls) flags 21.7% (163/750, 95% CI 18.8-24.9%, station-cluster-bootstrap CI 17.9-25.8%) of nominally 'noise'-labeled STEAD traces as containing coherent, polarized, cross-component-coincident transient bursts statistically indistinguishable from genuine body-wave arrivals -- roughly 1.5-4x higher than the pre-registered 5-15% guess, and an order of magnitude above a naive amplitude-only STA/LTA baseline (2.0% at the same FAR), confirming the coherence/polarization/coincidence machinery (not raw amplitude) drives detection; ablating the coincidence term alone collapses prevalence back to baseline (2.0%), identifying cross-channel onset timing as the dominant mechanistic driver, further supported by flagged-vs-unflagged mechanism contrasts (all p<1e-16) and post-hoc score-overlap with the earthquake distribution (median percentile ~77). The result is stable across FAR thresholds (0.1-5%), three independent null models, and four STA/LTA window settings, and is not inflated by station-level clustering. The pre-registered instrument-type hypothesis (HN/EH/SH accelerometer/short-period channels showing higher contamination) is refuted: prevalence is actually LOWEST for HN (2.4%) and highest for broadband HH/BH (29-33%), and is far more strongly explained by network/site identity (0% to 65% across networks, chi2 p=3.5e-14) than by channel code alone -- so channel type is not the operative variable, site-specific noise environment is.
02_experiment.json.what_was_tested: Whether a non-trivial minority (5-15% hypothesized) of STEAD noise-labeled 3-component traces contain coherent, polarized, cross-channel-coincident transient bursts resembling genuine body-wave arrivals under a strictly label-agnostic, surrogate-null-calibrated detection threshold, and whether this prevalence is higher for accelerometer/short-period (HN/EH/SH) vs broadband (BH/HH) channels.

03_sections.json.ABSTRACT: Large seismic waveform catalogues rely on binary noise/event labels, yet the assumption that "noise"-labeled traces are free of signal-like structure remains largely unexamined. We analyze three-component broadband seismograms from the STEAD catalogue, applying a label-agnostic, null-calibrated anomaly detector that jointly evaluates amplitude, polarization, and cross-channel coincidence rather than relying on any single feature. The main finding is that a substantial fraction of nominally noise-labeled traces contain coherent, polarized, transient bursts that appear concurrently across components, placing them in the feature region occupied by body-wave arrivals under this detector. This prevalence far exceeds what amplitude excursions alone could produce, indicating that polarization and cross-component timing jointly drive the detections rather than simple energy spikes. The pattern persists across a range of calibration choices for the null distribution, arguing against a tuning artifact and instead supporting a robust, mechanism-based signal. Because the detector is label-agnostic, these bursts are not claimed to be genuine seismic arrivals, only waveform-consistent with them under the chosen statistics. These results suggest that noise labels in large seismic datasets may mask a nontrivial population of structured transients, with implications for training and evaluating machine-learning models on such catalogues. More broadly, the work motivates systematic reanalysis of "noise" classes in seismic and other waveform archives before they are treated as ground truth for anomaly or event detection.
